summary: Gives an overview, threat analysis and requirements for the Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols effort. Existing authentication methods in routing protocols are often dated, vulnerable or use deprecated algorithms, and KARP aims to improve them. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Routing protocols let routers tell each other how to reach different parts of the internet, and most of them have a secret key that lets neighbours check each other's messages really came from a peer. RFC 6862 is the plan for making those checks stronger and easier to change. It says what attackers try to do, which attacks signing a message can and cannot stop, and what each routing protocol's specification must include to count as fixed.

questions: how to secure routing protocol authentication
why routing protocol authentication is weak
subtitle: The plan for making routing protocols harder to spoof, and the list of requirements each protocol must meet.

tldr.problem: The secret handshakes that routing protocols use to recognise each other are old, often use algorithms that are no longer strong, and are painful to rotate, so attackers can insert forged routes.
tldr.mechanism: KARP, the Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols effort, names the threats that per-packet authentication can address, says which are out of scope, and lists 21 requirements that routing protocol specifications must meet when they update their transport security.
tldr.outcome: The document is a roadmap, not a protocol. It asks for incremental improvement rather than a redesign, because deployed routers cannot run the strongest cryptography without a performance penalty operators will not accept.

today: RFC 6862 is an Informational RFC published in March 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the threat and requirements document for the KARP effort, one of two parts together with RFC 6518, and contains no protocol specifications of its own.

sections.title: Why Routing Protocols Need Better Secrets
sections.content:
In March 2006 the Internet Architecture Board held a workshop on unwanted internet traffic. The report from that workshop, RFC 4948, says that a simple risk analysis suggests an ideal attack target of minimal cost but maximal disruption is the core routing infrastructure, and calls for tightening the security of that infrastructure. Four steps were identified: create secure mechanisms and practices for operating routers, clean up the Internet Routing Registry repository and secure both the database and access to it, create specifications for cryptographic validation of routing message content, and secure the routing protocols' packets on the wire.

This RFC addresses the last of those four. More precisely, it focuses on securing the transport systems that routing protocols use, including the mechanisms built into the protocols themselves to authenticate packets. The effort is called Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols, or KARP. KARP is concerned with protecting the messages between directly communicating peers. That is distinct from making sure routing information is properly authorised relative to its source, which other mechanisms handle and which is outside this document.

This is one of two documents that together form the guidance for KARP design teams; the other is the KARP Design Guide, RFC 6518. Neither contains protocol specifications. This document defines where specification work is needed and sets the requirements that design teams must follow as they update a routing protocol's existing transport security.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF decided that the way routers recognise each other needed to be stronger. This RFC is the plan for that work: it names the attacks, says which ones signing each message can stop, and lists what each routing protocol must change to count as fixed.

sections.title: What KARP Covers and What It Leaves Out
sections.content:
Three basic principles can secure any piece of data as it crosses the network: confidentiality, authenticity and integrity. KARP focuses on message authentication and message integrity only. Confidentiality is explicitly excluded for now, as is non-repudiation. Since the aim of most routing protocols is to broadcast the routing topology widely, routing packets are commonly sent in the clear, and confidentiality is not normally needed for them. Making sure that routing peers are authentically identified, and that no rogue peer or unauthenticated packet can destabilise the routing environment, is critical and is in scope.

OSPF, IS-IS, LDP and RIP already have mechanisms that cryptographically authenticate and integrity-check their messages on the wire. Products and code that use those mechanisms exist and have been tuned for them. Rather than throw them away, this document aims to enhance them and bring them up to modern security levels.

The roadmap therefore has three parts. Work Phase 1 is making use of the existing transport security mechanisms where they have been specified, and enhancing or updating them to modern cryptographic practice. Work Phase 2 is a framework for automatic key management, so that keys can be deployed easily, cost less to run, and can be changed quickly when a breach happens, plus a specification of an automated key management protocol that can be combined with the routing protocol mechanisms. Both KARP documents set a direction, requirements and priorities rather than protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: KARP is about proving that a routing message really came from a neighbour and was not altered in transit. It is not about hiding routing traffic, and it is not about checking that the routes themselves are sensible. Those are separate jobs.

sections.title: Improving Things a Step at a Time
sections.content:
The principle is crawl, walk, run. A routing protocol's authentication may not go straight from its current state to the best possible state, because sometimes the best security available has to give way to security that is far better than today but not the best possible, so that progress towards a more secure internet still happens. There are practical reasons for this. Many deployed routers cannot run the most modern cryptography without a performance penalty that operators will not accept, and current routing performance has been tuned over twenty years of software and hardware work. New security changes that balance, so some specification elements may be introduced with SHOULD guidance, with the intention that the same mechanism carries a MUST in a later release.

The BGP work is the example given. Improving BGP security through the TCP Authentication Option would ideally have started with a fully specified key management protocol for negotiating the keying material, using certificates for peer authentication. Instead, in the spirit of incremental deployment, the IETF first addressed algorithm agility, replay attacks and the resetting of TCP sessions in the base protocol, and only later began to layer key management on top.

Operator interviews explain why. A survey reported in the RFC found that over 70 per cent of operators had deployed TCP MD5 on their external BGP sessions, over 55 per cent on their internal BGP connections, and 50 per cent on some other interior gateway protocol. Anecdotally, of those who had deployed TCP MD5 somewhere, only about 25 to 30 per cent of the routers in their network were deployed with the authentication enabled, and none reported using IPsec to protect the routing protocol. Operators using MD5 almost all reported using one manually distributed key throughout the entire network, and that the key had not been changed since it was installed, sometimes five or more years ago.

The reasons given are practical. Changing keys triggers a TCP reset, so links bounce and service level agreements are undermined. Coordinating a key change with another organisation is cumbersome and is done one peer or one autonomous system at a time. Keys must be changed at precisely the same time, or at least within 60 seconds as two major vendors support, to limit the outage. Key change is seen as a low priority, staff levels are insufficient to do it device by device, and the three kinds of operational peering, with other operators, within one operator, and with customer devices, are all reported to be cumbersome to manage securely. One operator reported using the same key for all customer equipment, and that creating a unique key on request caused such an operational headache that administrators now tell customers the option does not exist.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan is to improve routing security in steps rather than all at once, because routers already in service cannot do the strongest cryptography without slowing down. The RFC lists the reasons operators give for never rotating their keys: it drops sessions, it needs coordination with other organisations, and it has to happen on every device at the same moment.

sections.title: The Threats KARP Must and Must Not Address
sections.content:
KARP takes its threat model from the RFC on generic threats to routing protocols and sorts the threats into those in scope and those out of scope. The in-scope sources are outsiders, meaning anyone who is not a legitimate participant and who may be anywhere on the network; unauthorised key holders, meaning an attacker who has obtained keying material and can now pass an authentication check; terminated employees, who are a special case of the unauthorised key holder; and, as out of scope, Byzantine routers, which are faulty, misconfigured or subverted routers whose messages cause routing to malfunction.

Outsiders are split into on-path attackers, who control a network resource or a tap between two peers and can tamper with packets so that both peers believe they are talking to each other when they are talking to the attacker, and off-path attackers, who sit elsewhere and can launch active attacks such as spoofing or denial of service. The in-scope threat actions are spoofing, denial-of-service attacks at the transport layer or through the authentication mechanism itself, falsification of routing information by outsiders, and brute-force attacks against passwords and keys.

Several things are explicitly out of scope. Byzantine sources are excluded because KARP's job is to ensure that messages came from authorised peers and were not altered in transit, and a valid peer forming a bogus message is a different problem. Passive wiretapping is excluded, because preventing it is a job for encryption. So are interference by not forwarding packets, by delaying messages, by denying receipt, and unauthorised message content, which the SIDR working group covers, along with denial-of-service attacks that do not involve the routing protocol at all, such as a flood of traffic filling the link ahead of the router.
sections.plainLanguage: KARP is meant to catch attackers who are not real neighbours and forged messages sent from anywhere. It is not meant to catch a router that is broken or taken over, because a broken router can still sign its messages perfectly, and it is not meant to hide routing traffic from anyone watching.

sections.title: What Each Routing Protocol Has to Do
sections.content:
The RFC lists 21 requirements that a Work Phase 1 update to a routing protocol should meet, and recommends that the specification say how each one is met, with justification for any that are not. The first group is about the mechanism itself: a clear statement of which elements of the transmitted data are protected, strong algorithms accepted by the IETF security community, and algorithm agility with more than one algorithm specified so that a broken cipher can be replaced. Secure use of pre-shared keys is required, and the mechanism should detect and reject both intra-session and inter-session replay, including the case where a message is replayed with a different origin on a shared segment.

The second group is about keys over time. A change of security parameters must force a change of session traffic keys, and the mechanism must be able to rekey inside a session without disrupting it, ideally with a key identifier so the receiver can pick the right key. Keys must be installable and usable very quickly, which is what handles the reactive case where keys have already leaked, and the reactive case is why the terminated employee threat matters. A traffic key should never be a fixed value in a device configuration.

The third group is about the network around the mechanism. New mechanisms must resist denial-of-service attacks, and must not hide or encrypt the IP and transport header information that routers use to rate-limit unwanted control-plane traffic. Mandatory algorithms and default settings must be specified so that two operators who enable the mechanism with nothing but a pre-shared key can still connect. Convergence times should not be materially affected; an increase of more than 5 per cent is likely to be treated as material by operators. The mechanism should not cause extra route advertisements, should not interfere with the priority given to certain packets, and should send minimal information about itself in protocol packets. Every new mechanism must support incremental deployment: per-peer configuration, backward compatibility with unsecured peers, a way for secured routers to tell whether a peer meant to be secured, and a transition without service interruption.
sections.plainLanguage: The 21 requirements come down to a few ideas: use strong algorithms and be ready to swap them, catch replayed messages, let operators change keys quickly and without dropping sessions, keep the protection cheap enough to run on current routers, and let a network adopt it one router at a time without breaking.

sections.title: The Group Key Problem and What This Document Is
sections.content:
The security considerations section points to one problem that is not solved by the requirements. The use of a group key between a set of routing peers has special properties, because possession of the group key is what is used to validate identity and no other identity check is used. Under those conditions there is an attack when one peer masquerades as a neighbour using the neighbour's source IP address. This is well documented in the group-keying literature and is non-trivial to solve. Solutions exist within the group-keying realm, but they come with significant increases in complexity and computational intensity.

The document is mostly about security considerations for the KARP effort, both the threats and the requirements for addressing them, and points to the Security Considerations section of the KARP Design Guide for more detail. It records that the majority of the initial draft text was taken from an earlier roadmap for cryptographic authentication of routing protocol packets, and that the work was sponsored by Juniper Networks.
sections.plainLanguage: One problem remains unsolved. When a group of routers shares one key, that key is the only thing proving who is who, so a router in the group can pretend to be one of its neighbours. The RFC says the known fixes for that cost a lot of extra computation.

viz.caption: THREATS IN AND OUT OF SCOPE FOR KARP

cells: Falsification of routing information by outsiders
Message content validity, handled by the SIDR working group
Denial of service on the protocol or its authentication
A flood of traffic that fills the link ahead of the router
Brute-force attacks on passwords and keys
Unauthorised key holders, including terminated employees
Not forwarding, delaying messages, and denying receipt

items.title: Outsider on the path
items.text: Controls a router or tap between two peers and can tamper with packets.

items.title: Outsider off the path
items.text: Sits elsewhere on the network and can send spoofed packets or flood the link.

items.title: Unauthorised key holder
items.text: Has obtained keying material and can now pass an authentication check.

items.title: Terminated employee
items.text: Was given access to keys and no longer works there, so the keys must be changed fast.

items.title: Byzantine router
items.text: Faulty, misconfigured or subverted, and out of scope for KARP.

items.title: Algorithm agility
items.text: More than one strong algorithm, so a broken cipher can be replaced.

items.title: Replay protection
items.text: Catch messages replayed inside a session or carried over from an earlier one.

items.title: Fast key change
items.text: New keys installed quickly, and a change of parameters forces new session keys.

items.title: No disruption
items.text: Rekey inside a session without dropping it, and leave convergence time alone.

items.title: Incremental deployment
items.text: One router at a time, working with peers that have no protection.

items.title: Nothing hidden
items.text: Keep the IP and transport headers visible so unwanted traffic can still be filtered.
